ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Five identical right-angled triangles can be arranged so that their larger acute angles touch to form the star shown in the diagram. It is also possible to form a different star by arranging more of these triangles so that their smaller acute angles touch. How many triangles are needed to form the second star?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a five-pointed star-shaped pattern outlined by green line segments; it can be seen that it is formed by 5 congruent right triangles arranged around the center point; one acute-angle tip of each of these triangles is concentrated near the center point, surrounding one full circle. The problem states that what are adjacent in the figure are the larger acute angles of each right triangle. Reasoning: One full circle around a point is 360°. Because the larger acute angles of 5 congruent triangles just surround one full circle, each larger acute angle is 360° ÷ 5 = 72°. The sum of the two acute angles of a right triangle is 90°, so the smaller acute angle is 90° - 72° = 18°. For the second star shape, to make the smaller acute angles adjacent at the center, the number of triangles needed is 360° ÷ 18° = 20.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: the shown star is made from 5 congruent right triangles, and the acute tips of those triangles meet around one central point with no gap, forming a full turn. From the text, these touching angles are the larger acute angles of the triangles. Therefore each larger acute angle is 360°/5 = 72°. Since each triangle is right-angled, its two acute angles sum to 90°, so the smaller acute angle is 90° - 72° = 18°. For the second star, the smaller acute angles meet around a point, so the number of triangles needed is 360°/18° = 20.
